title: Debt snowball vs avalanche: choose a payment order
dek: Compare smallest-balance and highest-rate repayment using the same payment budget, while keeping essentials and every required minimum covered.
metaDescription: Compare debt snowball and avalanche with a worked first-month example, clear assumptions and checks for promotion dates and unaffordable minimums.

paragraphs: Debt snowball directs extra money to the smallest balance. Debt avalanche directs it to the highest interest rate. Both keep required minimums paid on every account. Under a simple fixed-rate model with the same total payments and no special fees, targeting the highest rate reduces interest cost; snowball prioritizes clearing a small account.

When three statements arrive together, the difficult decision is often not knowing the definitions. It is deciding whether one closed account matters more to you than a lower interest bill. Compare those outcomes separately rather than treating either method as a character test. This guide covers ordinary repayment planning, not debt settlement, insolvency or student-loan program selection.

body.heading: What changes, and what stays the same

left.label: Snowball
items: Order targets by starting balance, smallest first.
Direct extra money to the first target.
After payoff, move its payment to the next target.

right.label: Avalanche
items: Order targets by interest rate, highest first.
Direct extra money to the first target.
After payoff, move its payment to the next target.

body.heading: Before choosing either order
items: List each current balance, APR, required minimum and due date from the statement.
Record promotional end dates, deferred-interest terms, fees and any prepayment restrictions.
Set aside essential living costs and decide what extra amount is genuinely available.
Check that every required minimum is covered before directing extra money anywhere.
Choose a target order and write down the reason so you can review it later.
After each payment, check that it posted and update the account balance.

body.heading: Invented example: the same first-month budget
body.intro: Illustration only. Interest is added once at APR divided by 12, then payments are applied. Rates stay fixed, there are no fees or new charges, and minimums below are assumed fixed for this comparison.

body.heading: Follow one payment month all the way through
paragraphs: The total budget is $390: $190 in minimums plus $200 extra. The model adds $9, $50 and $20 interest respectively, leaving $609, $2,050 and $3,020 before payments. With snowball, payments are $230, $60 and $100. End balances are $379, $1,990 and $2,920.

With avalanche, payments are $30, $260 and $100. End balances are $579, $1,790 and $2,920. Both end the first month owing $5,289. The difference is where the remaining debt sits: avalanche has $200 less exposed to the 30% rate and $200 more exposed to 18%. In the next model month, that allocation produces $2 less interest, before any later payoff changes.

This is a reproducible first-month comparison, not a complete payoff forecast. It does not establish how large the final gap will be. Real cards may calculate interest daily and change minimums; loan payment allocation can differ. Do not attach exact payoff dates to this simplified example.

body.heading: Compare cost, milestones and cash-flow relief
paragraphs: For a full comparison, hold the total payment budget constant, declare when interest and payments occur, and decide how leftover money in a payoff month moves to the next account. Apply the same rule to both schedules. Check total interest, the first account payoff and the last payment separately.

A closed account removes its required minimum, but the plan only accelerates if you keep directing that freed money to debt. You may instead need it for essentials after an income change. That is a cash-flow decision, not a failure of arithmetic. A hybrid approach can be reasonable if you understand its cost; it is not automatically the best of both methods.

The [CFPB explanation](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-reduce-your-debt/) describes both approaches and their tradeoffs. It does not supply a universal dollar threshold for choosing motivation over interest savings. Decide using your own priorities and circumstances, not a claim that everyone abandons one particular method.

body.heading: Pause the comparison when the assumptions fail
paragraphs: If minimums are unaffordable, choosing a target is not the next problem to solve. Contact creditors about available arrangements and seek reputable debt advice. Do not use money needed for food, housing or essential services simply to preserve a repayment chart.

A promotion expiring soon, deferred interest, a delinquent account, a secured debt at risk or a legal notice can require a different priority. Read the actual terms and get qualified help where needed. Review the plan when rates, balances or income change. For a payment already missed, start with [what to do next](/guides/you-missed-a-payment-what-to-do-next).

items.q: Does avalanche always clear debt faster?
items.a: Not necessarily by a different whole month, even when it reduces interest. Exact timing depends on balances, payment amounts, rates and rounding. It can also take longer to close the first account. Compare first payoff, final payoff and interest separately using identical assumptions for both schedules.

items.q: Can I switch from snowball to avalanche?
items.a: Yes. Keep required payments current and redirect future extra payments according to the revised order. Recheck promotional terms and account restrictions first. Record why you changed the plan so the next review is based on your priorities, rather than repeatedly switching because one statement felt discouraging.

items.q: Is a regular extra payment better than a lump sum?
items.a: For the same total contribution, earlier payments generally reduce interest sooner in a simple interest-bearing model. Regular payments may be easier to sustain, but that is a practical consideration, not proof they always save more. Compare equal totals over the same period and do not risk essential bills.
